title: Comparison Operators and Boolean Results
learningObjectives: Explain the key idea in comparison operators and boolean results.
Identify the relevant syntax and rules.
Trace each example and predict the result.
Apply the concept in a small program.
Avoid a common mistake related to this topic.

understand.concept: Comparison operators compare values and produce a boolean result. Equality and inequality compare for a relationship; relational operators compare ordering. A comparison is often used to control a decision.
understand.whyItMatters: Comparisons allow programs to test ranges, eligibility, matching values and stopping conditions.
understand.analogy: Think of this as a control or calculation rule that tells a program how to handle a particular situation consistently.
understand.analogyLimit: The analogy is only a starting point; C++ syntax, types and execution rules determine actual behaviour.
understand.explain:
## Comparisons
Use `==`, `!=`, `<`, `>`, `<=` and `>=` to compare values. Equality is written with two equals signs; one equals sign assigns.

## Boolean result
A comparison evaluates to `true` or `false`. Stream output prints bool as 1 or 0 unless formatting with `std::boolalpha` is enabled.

## Floating-point comparisons
Exact equality may be unsuitable for calculated floating-point values. For measurements, consider a tolerance appropriate to the problem.

practise.guidedTask: Choose one example from this lesson. Predict its result before running it, change one input or condition, predict again, then explain the difference. Compile and test locally if a C++ compiler is available.
practise.independentTask: Write a small C++ program that demonstrates comparison operators and boolean results in a meaningful scenario. Include at least two test cases and explain how the code behaves at boundaries or unexpected inputs.

options: They can reveal off-by-one or unexpected behaviour
They make code longer without benefit

questions.answer: They can reveal off-by-one or unexpected behaviour
questions.explanation: Boundary tests help reveal mistakes at the limits of expected inputs or conditions.
